20.1 i ntroduction
Confidence intervals can be used as an alternative for hypothesis testing in business decision
making. A hypothesis test is usually a yes-no decision. We either reject a hypothesis or fail
to reject it. A confidence interval not only gives that answer, but it also provides information
about the possible range of values for the parameter.
Confidence intervals are in general easier to understand and explain to decision makers than
hypothesis tests. In this chapter, we will review hypothesis testing situations and resolve
those situations with confidence intervals.
20.2 c hoosing a c onfidence Level
Often we have used confidence levels of 90% or 95% in our illustrations and examples. In
reality, these confidence levels are not the only values used. The choice of the confidence
level is based on the loss one would sustain if the parameter is outside the range and the gain
one would have if the parameter is inside the range. If the loss is high compared to the gain,
the confidence levels should be high. If the loss is negligible compared to the gain, a lower
confidence level is fine.
In general, one must be cautious when interpreting confidence levels. When reviewing a
research article with a 60% confidence level, do not make the assumption that the confi-
dence is low and conclude that it is not worthy of making a decision based upon the underly-
ing parameter. Even if the parameter is significant at the 99% confidence level, it is possible
for decision makers to say that the confidence level is not high enough if the loss due to
wrong decisions is large.

20.3 Hypothesis t esting versus c onfidence i ntervals
Rather than just a simple yes-no decision, as encountered with hypothesis tests, confidence
intervals also provide the possible range of values for the parameter. A narrow confidence
interval indicates that the parameter has been estimated with a high degree of precision.
Wide confidence intervals indicate that a low precision is involved in the yes-no decision
making. Decision makers often need to know the precision rather than or in addition to the
simple yes-no answers in testing. When testing the null hypothesis that the means from two
samples are the same and we have a [–50, 50] confidence interval for the difference in the
population means, we can state there is no difference between the means since the interval
includes zero. But think how much stronger the result would be if the confidence interval
was [–1, 1].
Management is usually more receptive to confidence intervals since they are visual, making
them easier to understand and communicate. Clearly it would be easier to comprehend that
a parameter is in a specific range than to know that the probability of the parameter being
one specific value is less than a specified percentage.

To obtain meaningful results, these guidelines should be followed when using the chi-square
test of independence:
1. For contingency tables with two rows and two columns, the average expected cell
frequency should be at least 7.5.
2. For contingency tables with equal expected cell frequencies throughout, the expected
cell frequencies should be at least 2 when a = 5% and at least 4 when a = 1%.
3. For contingency tables with unequal expected cell frequencies, the average expected
cell frequency should be at least 6 when a = 5% and at least 10 when a = 1%.
4. The number of expected cell frequencies equal to 0 should be minimized, not by
collapsing rows or columns but by taking sufficiently large samples.
Many mathematicians simply state that in any chi-square test of independence, every
expected cell frequency should be at least 5.
In our example, the average expected cell frequency is 11.67, which justifies the use of the
chi-square test by rule 3.

23.1 i ntroduction
The chi-square test is used to test if a sample of data came from a population with a specific
distribution.
An attractive feature of the chi-square goodness-of-fit test is that it can be applied to any
univariate distribution for which you can calculate the cumulative distribution function. The
chi-square goodness-of-fit test is applied to binned data (i.e., data put into classes). This is
actually not a restriction since for non-binned data you can simply calculate a histogram or
frequency table before generating the chi-square test. However, the value of the chi-square
test statistic is dependent on how the data is binned. Note that the chi-square test requires a
sufficient sample size in order for the chi-square approximation to be valid. In this chapter,
we will conduct a chi-square test of goodness-of-fit and a hypothesis test on missing data.
23.2 c hi-s quare t ests of g oodness-of-f it
We can use a chi-square test based on the comparison of expected and observed frequencies
to test whether a sample could have come from a population with a specified distribution.
Such a test is called a goodness-of-fit test (or a one-sample chi-square test) and can be used to
test the normality of a population involved in a t-test or to determine if the values produced
by a random number generator are, in fact, selected from a uniform distribution. In general,
these hypotheses are tested:
H
0
: The sample is from a population having a specified distribution.
H
a
: The population is from some other distribution.

Regression and Curve Fitting
A CER is a mathematical expression, expressing cost as a function of one or more cost driv-
ing variables. In fact, the problem is that the CER complexity increases as one moves from
linear to non-linear relationship, and from a single cost driver to more than one cost driver.
But today, the necessary algorithms are well-known and widely available. The main meth-
ods to curve fitting are the multivariate regression techniques and cost improvement curve
analysis. With the use of modern computer tools, it is possible to automatically investigate
and test many combinations of CER’s mathematical forms (linear, logarithm, exponential).
One can also use more advanced black-box modeling techniques such as neural networks if
the loss of the readability of the cost model is acceptable.
Test of the CERs Statistical Quality
Finally, we must verify the significance and accuracy of the cost estimation models through
various statistical tests. The choice of the cost drivers can be statistically established and
tested here. The CER can be simplified by selecting only the most statistically significant
terms, for example by using stepwise regression techniques.
Selection of the Best CER
At this point, it is usual to obtain a great number of candidate models. In many cases, the
statistical regression quality and estimation criteria are not sufficient. For their validation,
the CERs must demonstrate reliability for an acceptable number of trials, and they should
be representative of the database domain of application. It is also necessary to consider the
technical coherence of the CER as defined by the experts in the application domain. At
last, some input variables in the multiple regression do not have an important explanatory
effect on the response. Then, it is a convenient simplification to keep only the statistically
significant cost drivers in the model. The stepwise regression starts with all the terms in the
model and removes the least significant terms until all the remaining terms are statistically
significant. It is also possible to start with a subset of all the terms and then add significant
terms or remove insignificant.

24.1 Introduction
In Unit 5, we saw that the chi-square test of independence can be used to detect a relation-
ship between two variables. When such a test reveals a dependence, however, it tells us noth-
ing about the nature of the relationship. Is it strong or weak? Do large values of one variable
generally correspond to large or small values of the other? In this chapter, we will develop
numerical measures of the correlation between the values of two variables.

24.2 Scatter Diagrams
We have seen how useful histograms can be in visualizing the distribution of the values of
a variable. Similarly, we can create a graphical display of the values of two variables that

scatter diagrams, and are formed by plotting in the XY plane points whose coordinates are
the paired values of the two variables. When one variable is thought to be dependent on the
other, the values of the dependent variable are plotted along the vertical (Y) axis, while the

The reader should be aware that the presence of a significant correlation between the values
of two variables does not necessarily imply that a cause-and-effect mechanism links them.
They might both be influenced by some third quantity, or their apparent connection might
be a numerical coincidence. A significant correlation tells us only that some physical interac-
tion might be present and that its possibility should be investigated.
